newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador seeks U.S.-style Galapagos immigration law.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador seeks U.S.-style Galapagos immigration law.

text.p: Ecuador has begun promoting a new immigration law for the Galapagos Islands to protect the islands' delicate ecosystem, a government official said on Friday.

"We want to stop more people from going there, which is why we are creating four categories: permanent residents, temporary residents, tourists and passers-by," Environment Undersecretary Juan Carlos Paez told Reuters.

The Galapagos, off the Pacific coast of Ecuador, form a unique ecosystem that inspired 19th century naturalist Charles Darwin's theory of evolution. But damage to native species earlier this year led UNESCO to threaten dropping them from its list of World Heritage Sites.

Paez said President Fabian Alarcon would send Congress an immigration law on Aug. 30 that is likely to be passed within 60 days. It will classify people born on the islands or living there at least five years as permanent residents, as opposed to those with temporary work contracts.
"Temporary residents will be able to work only as stated in their contracts. They won't be allowed to carry out any other economic activity," Paez said. "It's similar to the U.S. immigration law."

Tourists will be allowed to visit for up to 90 days and may renew their visas once. Some 50,000 people visit the archipelago each year against a stable population of 14,000, which inhabits only 3 percent of the islands.

"Immigration is primarily the result of the tourism boom. Tourism requires services, which requires workers," Paez said. He noted electricity, water, telephones and gasoline are subsidised on the islands.
